This study examines how a Poisson Wold-AR model can be enhanced to better capture the dynamic relationships in multivariate time series data, with the improved version called the TV-POIR model allowing for the investigation of time-varying correlations and the potential for seasonal patterns in the data.

Unexpectedly, this research found that aerosol optical depth can be effectively estimated using existing technology intended for wide-angle stellar photometry. This method, in particular the Deep Learning based --SDS-+-SDS-+-DCN-+-DCN-+-model, was found to be highly accurate and robust against cloud interference, outperforming existing systems derived from wide-field imaging. The model's simplicity also allowed for easy use with existing wide-field cameras intended for astronomical purposes. By leveraging this model, researchers could monitor large areas efficiently and potentially integrate it with existing telescopes for both real-time monitoring and in-flight observations. The team also proposed designing a new type of wide-field telescope specifically optimized for real-time aerosol monitoring.

Reconstructing a damaged protein structure is akin to a high-dimensional optimization task, similar to finding a peak on a rugged landscape with many local maxima. To effectively perform this optimization, we've developed an updated method that incorporates a unique molecular time step and external forces, such as gravity and diffusion, into the Langevin dynamics simulation. Our enhancement also sees the elimination of a fixed time step in favor of a adaptive approach, allowing us to achieve faster and more reliable structure repairs. Using multiple benchmarks, including CATH database domains, PDB-ranged structures, and difficult examples, our newly optimized method has demonstrated its superiority over existing techniques. Additionally, it aligns well with the theoretical Samplers Theorem, ensuring reliable configurational sampling when sufficient simulation time is used.

Recent advances in low-cost automatic image description generation have sparked interest in evaluating the quality of such outputs. Currently, assessing the quality of image descriptions is often done through agreement among a small group of people, but this method is time-consuming and not representative of how real users judge descriptions. To address this, we explore the use of human reference material for evaluation purposes. Our hypothesis is that the effectiveness of describing an image can be improved if a human reference is used prior to generating a description, and we validate this by conducting two experiments. The first experiment involves a existing dataset of videos with descriptions, and the second requires participants to view and optionally describe 100 images. Our findings reveal that human reference-based evaluation is an efficient and unbiased method for assessing image description generation, and that descriptions are more effective when created with prior viewing of the content. Additionally, we provide a large dataset of 20,000 images for future research.

We provide a comprehensive summary of research showing that several seemingly unrelated mathematical concepts are actually equivalent. These concepts include intrinsic curvature squared in geometric quantization, the rate of change of a symplectic area in Hamiltonian mechanics, and the non-abelian bracket of vector fields on a manifold. This profound connection reveals that these theories are deeply interconnected. We then explore how this relationship can be extended to higher-order equations and discuss its significance. Additionally, we present a novel higher-order geometric field theory and derive its equation of motion, demonstrating that it leads to a 5th-order integer master equation. We provide a similar interpretation of this equation and offer several other perspectives on its meaning.

Recent observations of dark matter have led to the consideration of ultra-light particles, such as axions and similar bosons, as possible components of it. To evaluate if these particles can account for the observed dark matter halo around the Milky Way, an effective field theory is employed to eliminate model-specific details. This approach derives relationships between the production of these particles and the phase transitions that occurred in the early universe, including symmetry breaking, thermal equilibrium, and possibly even first-order transitions. To determine the total mass of these particles per galaxy, the relations are combined with both established and cutting-edge cosmological data, resulting in the visualization of fulfillment of phase transition conditions and the calculation of masses. It is argued that considering the uncertainty in the velocity dispersion profile of the Milky Way, it may be necessary to account for clumping of these ultra-light particles when determining their total mass within a galaxy. To ensure that theoretical predictions align with observed data, it is suggested that future models should incorporate more accurate descriptions of the early universe, as well as better observations of the Milky Way. Additionally, it is proposed that a non-equilibrium state of the universe during the one-percent symmetry breaking phase may be described using a non-constant order parameter.

This article presents streamlined versions of a multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) broadband waveforming technique called BWB-WF, designed for single-antenna systems. The BWB-WF is an advanced signal processing method that leverages multiple carriers and multiple antennas, specifically BWB-OFDM, to optimize data rates and power transfer efficiency. In single-antenna setups, achieving BWB-OFDM's performance can be challenging due to inter-carrier interference (ICI) management. To overcome this, we developed two precoding strategies based on existing techniques SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM, called SISO-OFDM-EQ and MISO-OFDM-EQ, that mimic BWB-OFDM's behavior. The primary contribution of this research is the mathematical derivation showing how to calculate the optimal power allocation and precoding matrices for both approaches to maximize transfer efficiency. Applying these formulas to practical scenarios demonstrates that while multiple-carrier and multiple-waveforming methods offer significant benefits, their improvements diminish as the number of carriers and antennas increases. In addition, the article compares the performance of all four precoding schemes across various system configurations, highlighting the factors that influence their effectiveness.

We present a flexible theory framework that allows for the precise adjustment of parton distribution functions (PDFs) at any given scale. Our approach is based on the projection method, which we've extended to incorporate a novel matching strategy between the adjusted and the unadjusted PDFs. This ensures that PDF momentum is conserved throughout the adjustment process. Our framework is user-friendly, enabling the incorporation of both experimental data and non-perturbative QCD calculations to generate customized PDF sets at any scale of interest. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we've used it to generate multiple adjusted PDF sets at various scales and employed them in next-leading order QCD calculations of experimental observables, showing a strong agreement with existing experimental data.

This study examines the interaction between a turbulent jet fire and an externally applied acoustic force acting on the base of the jet, utilizing linearized RANS equations to predict the resulting deformations and fluctuations. The simulation incorporates RANS-based turbulence modeling, linearized turbulence and heat flux equations, and directly resolves the applied acoustic force. To accurately capture the application of the acoustic force, the approach abandons standard inflow boundary conditions in favor of an active flame strategy that allows the force to shape the flame's dynamics at the inlet. The effectiveness of the simulation is validated by comparing the results to established experimental data, demonstrating the method's capacity to accurately recreate both the typical flame behavior and its response to external acoustic influence.

This work extends the nonlocal gravity framework by integrating the concepts of a constitutive connection and a metric tensor, allowing nonlocal field equations to describe self-gravitating systems accurately.

This paper discusses tiny computing systems suitable for use in exotic and transient particle detectors being considered for discovery-grade searches at the LHC. It outlines the unique challenges these systems face and outlines possible solutions.

Observations of some Galactic Centre X-ray binaries have shown a possible link between the type of neutron star and how often it shows outbursts. To test this, we examined the data on X-ray binary outbreak repetition intervals (RIs) and found a median RI of 11 years. This is comparable to the observed magnetic field reduction timescale of pulsars but significantly longer than the radiative cooling timescale of magnetars, suggesting that the initial strength of the neutron star's magnetic field may determine outbreak frequency. Additionally, we proposed that the dormant X-ray binaries with low or uncertain neutron star masses in the Galactic Centre likely have weak magnetic fields and that the burst activity of the Galactic Centre X-ray binaries may be influenced by the neutron star's magnetic field strength, along with other possible factors such as the binary system's inclination and the presence of an accretion disk instability driven by neutron-cpair superfluidity in the core. The discovery that the outbreak frequency of X-ray binaries may be related to the strength of the neutron star's magnetic field opens up the possibility of estimating magnetic field strengths of distant burst X-ray stars and provides a basis for exploring the connection between magnetic fields and accretion dynamics. This in turn may lead to searching for oscillation signals, such as $g$-mode and $r$-mode, in the superfluid core of the neutron star, and the continuous wave emission resulting from the star's irregular shape or rotation speed variations. Bipartite graphs are structured as two distinct sets of vertices, where edges only connect across the sets. Fault-tolerant configurations are faultless setups that maintain specified properties even when some vertices are removed. This research focuses on dividing a bipartite graph into two parts so that the resulting subgraphs are both 0.5-resilient and have no edges between them. It is shown that if an FPT algorithm can determine whether a given graph meets the required conditions in relation to the number of failing vertices, then it is possible to efficiently partition the graph into two distinct sets that satisfy the specified requirements, even when a small percentage of the graph's potential connections are missing or corrupted.

A cutting-edge side-channel attack called "Degrade" enables hardware vendors to reduce a system's speed by up to 99.9% through fault injection without altering the hardware. However, this method is limited by slow execution speeds following the fault injection. Our new approach, HyperDegrade, builds on Degrade and significantly enhances its effectiveness by combining multiple types of side-channels, specifically last-level cache timing and branch prediction vulnerabilities. We achieved speed reductions of up to three orders of magnitude following the fault injection compared to the Degrade technique. As a result, we were able to decrease an Intel Xeon E5-2697 v4 system's performance by 99.999% through HyperDegrade, without compromising the system's functionality, in contrast to the unattainable goals of the Degrade approach. Furthermore, we applied HyperDegrade sequentially to the same system, cumulatively decreasing its performance by five orders of magnitude in a three-stage process, again without compromising the system's functionality. This multi-stage approach could be particularly useful for safety-critical applications, although we didn't explore it in this study.

We present a new unknotting method for traditional and welded knots that iteratively reduces the number of crossings in a knot or link diagram by generating a sequence of modified diagrams with fewer crossings. The process involves four steps: picking a knot angle, modifying the knot through pulling or flipping, continuing with the modified diagram, and concluding when a sequence of monoid operations reduces the knot's complexity. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this unknotting procedure on several example knots and links, prove its validity for traditional knots using existing theorems and a specific lemma, and discuss its limitations for 2-braid knots. Additionally, we introduce a variation of the process for welded knots that incorporates additional diagram modifications.

In dynamic environments where computation and communication are limited, we develop a collaborative strategy for role-based robotic teams operating in a 3D space. As the team scales, we optimize the collaborative approach to conserve computation and time. We propose a hierarchical structure that enables the team to locate and identify buried targets efficiently. Our method involves dividing the team into levels, with the top tier searching broadly and the lower tiers scanning in greater detail when a promising area is found. We validate our collaborative model through computer simulations that demonstrate its effectiveness in locating targets with high precision and speed.

This paper explains how a specific type of mathematical group, called a surface group with a Euclidean structure, can be integrated into a specific type of mathematical structure known as a Garland product.

The detection capabilities of gravitational wave detectors are hindered by the limited sensitivity of optical sensors at high frequencies. The sloshing Sagnac interferometer, a novel design that reconfigures the basic setup by stacking and linking multiple optical Michelson interferometers in a planar arrangement through the use of recycled optics and an additional beam splitting component in an asymmetric design, has been found to potentially address this restriction. Theoretical analysis and numerical simulations indicate that the asymmetric design of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer results in the cancellation of the side coupling effect observed in conventional recycled interferometers, leading to the formation of dark and bright modes with distinct squeezing characteristics. The dark mode of the sloshing Sagneng interferemon exhibits exponential growth towards radiation pressure Squeezing as the frequency increases, in contrast to the power-law pattern displayed by the bright mode of the bright mode of the interferometer. In addition, the sloshing Sagnac interferometer demonstrates enhanced sensitivity to gravitational waves through the utilization of quantum entanglement reconstruction techniques, thereby showcasing its potential for improving the detection capabilities of the devices. The unique features of the sloshing Sagnac design make it a promising candidate for the future multi-kiloton scale gravitational wave detectors, and further study of the design may lead to the cancellation of the dark-bright mode cancellation pattern observed in recycled Michelson interferometers.

Recent large-scale MIMO systems have seen rapid development and are considered a key technology for next-generation wireless networks. As a result, non-intersecting visible SLICs in XL-MIMO STPCA protocols have gained significant interest and are crucial for non-interlapping STPCAs. This research aims to investigate the distribution of non-intersecting visibility SLICs in a XL-MIMO stochastic access protocol, observing the following key findings: the total probability of non-intersecting SLICs increases as the data rate in XL-MIMO stochastic access protocols decreases and is also influenced by the user distribution and network size. In addition, the paper proposes an optimal data rate that maximizes the total probability of non-intersecting SLICs in XL-MIMO stochastic access protocols. Furthermore, it is discovered that the best non-intersecting STPCAs occur when the user distribution is uniform, and the decision to increase the XL-MIMO transmit array size from 100 to 400 elements has little impact on the total probability of non-intersecting visibility regions. These observations contribute to the design of scalable and energy-efficient XL-MIMO networks.

Neural networks have largely replaced $n$-gram models in language modeling due to the need for more complex architectures. However, we find that simply extending an neural network's output layer with an $N$-gram model can significantly enhance performance with minimal computational cost and no need for deeper or more complex network designs. In our experiments on large-scale corpora like Wikipedia, we observe that residual learning of $n$-gram loss can dramatically improve neural network performance, with $MERIT$-measured evaluations showing similar gains in less balanced corpora. We propose that the high-dimensional space of language allows both complex network structures and $n$-gram constraints to effectively capture linguistic patterns, and that our proposed combination of the two yields even better results.

This investigation in the realm of optical character recognition (OCR) technology introduces an approach that incorporates geometric information to enhance the precision of symbol recognition systems. The proposed modified strategy, that integrates geometric cues into the training process, has been found to deliver superior results when compared to existing methods, particularly in the absence of gold-standard annotations during the training phase. The underlying data set utilized for evaluating the improved approach consists of 14 distinct configurations representing various ballot design layouts. The proposed method in conjunction with unsupervised symbol recognition systems has been found to yield the highest levels of precision, recall, and F1 scores when utilized to automate ballot tabulation processes. The underlying code and models developed during this investigation are made available publicly for further use and exploration.

A simplified computational model was used to study and document the circulation patterns of super-rotating二氧化碳 atmospheres and icy atmospheres around planets and dwarf planets, considering a wide range of planetary conditions. By analyzing the results using a unified framework that takes into consideration the forces acting on the atmosphere (Coriolis, pressure gradient, and centrifugal forces), circulation patterns were categorized based on the balance of these forces under steady-state conditions. A new measure, the parameter Omega, was introduced to quantify the relative significance of centrifugal and Coriolis effects. Using this parameter, observed flow patterns, such as jet streams, circulation cells, and boundary layers, can be explained in a consistent manner. Specifically, the centrifugal force is found to be dominant near a planet's equator, giving rise to cyclostrophic jet streams, while the Coriolis force prevails near the poles, resulting in geostrophic jet streams. A transitional region where these forces are in balance gives rise to various circulation cells. In addition to these findings, the model also provides new insights into the application of different atmospheric stability metrics, the scattering of radiation by二氧化碳 ice particles, and the generation of turbulence by the Coriolis effect. A phase diagram was created to visualize the conditions under which different atmospheric flow patterns are predicted to occur, taking into consideration a planet's rotation speed, atmospheric conditions, and the characteristics of the atmosphere in question.

This study presents a new integral formulation of the reciprocal Gamma function that overcomes singularities at non-positive integers by incorporating a regularization parameter. The derived formula validates the reflection formula and connects to existing integral representations, including the Golubkov-Hegmon and Golubkov-Hegmon-Orszag formulations, through mathematical proof. Furthermore, the regularized integral formulation yields fresh expressions for the Gamma function's product and power functions. The underlying mathematical model has significant implications for applied fields, particularly statistical physics and chemistry, where the Gamma function is frequently used in distribution functions and other contexts. The smoothed integral formulation also facilitates numerical computations of the function.

Our developed methodology enables us to apply the Keldysh field-theoretic approach to investigate the dynamics of interacting Bose fluids within a random quantum hydrodynamic model, utilizing Phase-space Gaussian Mappings. By employing a closed-loop integral expression for the four-point correlation function, we can derive a approximate two-point function, resulting in a usable Dyson equation for the spectral function. Our Monte-Carlo simulation demonstrates good agreement with Exact Numerical Iterative Scheme results, indicating that our Approximate Dyson Equation method effectively captures the dynamics of Bose fluids.

Artificial intelligence in education has grown significantly, particularly in subject-area knowledge integration. Our comprehensive review incognito KFAIF provides a novel framework for knowledge incorporation from external sources based on the Instructor-Pupil Model. This model distinguishes itself through a collaborative interaction between an advanced AI and an external agent, contrasting with traditional methods. The process involves three main stages: external knowledge preparation, sequential model learning and refinement, and final knowledge verification and organization, each with unique strategies. Furthermore, we examine various applications of the framework across diverse NLP tasks, exploring its potential and limitations, as well as several implementation examples. The knowledge-graph based organization and its integration with large-scale language models are also discussed in detail, paving the way for future innovations.

We provide an concise summary of our paper, which presents exact and approximate methods for calculating the marginal probability of an entity of interest in a graphical model. Both exact and approximate optimization of a target function involve a form of dynamic programming known as message passing. Our approach builds on an established technique called Belief Propagation, incorporating a notion of rounding that allows for precise calculation of target functions when used in combination with Belief Propagation. Our contribution facilitates more accurate optimization of target functions, even in deeply interconnected graphical models where traditional methods like Belief Propagation may produce inaccurate results. Our technique is particularly useful in situations where optimizing a function requires a precise understanding of local probabilities within the model.

Recently introduced is a higher rank Lie algebra variant named the $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ stabilizer algebra, and the $n$-th commutant of the U(n) algebra within the U(n+n) algebra, which we demonstrate are in fact identical. This connection enables a novel perspective on the U(n) commutant algebra, now referred to as the $Z_n(\mathrac{sl}_2)$ algebra, facilitating an explicit calculation of its Hilbert-Poincaré polynomial, now termed the Catalan-Gotthilg polynomial, for any given n and any value of a parameter t. Furthermore, this novel approach extends to determining these polynomial sequences for any initial four operators similar to $h,e,f$. This technique is also applicable to higher rank Lie algebras beyond the $\mathfrac{sl}_2$ algebra, including the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ algebra, and even the general $\mathfrak{sl}_{n}$ algebra, in a straightforward manner. In the case of the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ algebra, it is shown that the $Z_3(\mathfrak{sl}_3)$ algebra is in fact identical to the Racah algebra $B_2$, revealing a deeper connection between these mathematical structures.

Paired-Permutation (PP) tests are commonly used in evaluating the effectiveness of algorithms for reducing bias in hiring. A key component of these tests is the measurement of how biased hiring decisions are, which is calculated based on the output of the algorithm in question. In a more precise variant called Structured Test Metrics (STM), candidates are assessed on their potential for bias reduction through a selection of tailored resumes for a given job. The lack of a universally accepted metric for determining the bias-reduction effectiveness of resumes has resulted in unclear specifications for the optimization problem. To address this, a new optimization problem is defined that focuses on minimizing the decision bias exhibited by an algorithm under examination. A suitable measure of how biased decisions are, known as a paired-permutation metric, is then required to evaluate the outcomes of the optimization process. Consequently, a more accurate way of assessing how reduced bias is achieved, derived from the Rank-Biased Measure (RBM), is needed. After several attempts, a better option called Precise Paired-Permutation (PPP) is identified and validated to effectively measure the reduction in bias exhibited by the optimization process.

Our research examined the connection between initial collision asymmetry and triangular flow $v_3$ in heavy ion collisions through a theoretical model, focusing on Au+Au, Cu+Cu, and Al+Al systems at 200 GeV. We found that the initial asymmetry in these collisions directly influences triangular flow, with a notable increase in $v_3}/{v_2}$ as the asymmetry grows. Additionally, we observed that a small initial ellipticity can still result in a measurable triangular flow. Our results also showed that a phase transition in the medium produced during collisions amplifies the anisotropic flow of particles, and when comparing our findings to experimental data from Cu+Cu and Au+Au collisions, we found the model's predictions aligned well with observations, particularly for the system size of 10% of central collisions and beyond.

This study presents a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter where the lattice-based birth model incorporates a lattice structure in its probability histogram. Additionally, a sub-optimal lattice reduction strategy is introduced to constrain the support set. Compared to previous lattice-based models, the proposed approach offers enhanced precision without compromising efficiency. The effectiveness of the new model and filter is validated through simulations.

This study is set against soccer match situations where outcomes are uncertain, exploring the use of automated decision support systems for players' management, specifically in determining the best times to substitute players or press the referee for penalty area changes. The research uses a reinforcement learning framework, developing a state representation that accounts for game dynamics and psychological factors, and employing a deep neural network for decision-making. To evaluate the strategy, simulated scenarios are used that reflect real-world playoff situations, assessing performance based on win probabilities and comparing results to random management and typical playoff conditions.

The expansion of LDV systems to two dimensions presents technical challenges, particularly in achieving a sufficient measurement area with a single-point system. In laboratory settings, optical alignment is time-consuming and space-consuming. This paper proposes a method to create a two-dimensional LDV system from a single-point laser Doppler anemometer system by utilizing a short arm of the interferometer to form a small remote reflection surface through a mirror, resulting in a two-dimensional measurement area at the tip of the short arm. The effectiveness of this configuration is validated through both theoretical analysis and experimental verification, demonstrating the creation of a two-dimensional LDV system from a single-point system and the occurrence of curvature in the LDV system's trace due to the increasing angle of remote reflection. This curvature can be corrected, and the proposed single-point LDV system's 2D configuration is found to be space-saving, flexible, and easy to adjust compared to traditional two-dimensional systems, making it particularly suitable for confined or irregular experimental areas.

We provide explicit definitions for the spectral and orbital stability of a system consisting of the Klein-Gordon equation and an anharmonic oscillator, based on boundary conditions. This system is of interest in the context of particle physics and mathematical studies of coupled systems. Our work clarifies the connection between spectral properties at the origin and the spectral and orbital integrity of the system. Additionally, we introduce precise conditions for both types of stability.

In experiments involving particle collisions, identifying neutral long-lived particles relies on either finding decay products at unusual locations or missing energy. The choice between these methods depends on the particle's properties, but for broad searches like in beauty quantum fluctuations, practical limitations make combining them difficult. To address this, we propose a new method that uses specific particle collisions involving radiative decays to find axion-like particles in Belle II's algorithm-driven search. This approach depends only on detecting the axion-like particle if it decays within the detector's range, eliminating the need for complex reconstruction of displaced decays and significantly enhancing the experiment's efficiency. This new strategy yields the most sensitive search for axion-like particles from beauty quantum fluctuations, surpassing previous results from supersymmetric particle searches like $D0$ and $BFactory$ like Belle, and often producing novel limits or measurements.

This study investigates the effectiveness of MBERT and Bi-Encoder models in identifying meaningful word changes within semantically significant contexts. A novel dataset, specifically designed for this purpose and termed ConWSD, has been Merged with existing alteration-based training data, including RTE and NER, to enhance the ConWSD data's diversity. When ConWSD was used as the sole training set, both MBERT and Bi-Encoder demonstrated poor initial results, though significant improvements were observed following the integration of additional, compounded training data. Ultimately, Contextualized Merged environments yielded the best outcomes, establishing that MBERT and Bi-Encoder can effectively discern meaningful changes in words, and thus, be utilized for more intricate, semantic training tasks.

Active galactic nucleus spin measurements can help narrow down the mass range of ultralight bosons through a specific growth mechanism. A Bayesian inference method is used to determine the constraints this growth mechanism provides on the boson mass range, with or without considering the specific type of AGN activity. To improve the effectiveness of this inference, a model is developed that combines different AGN activity drivers, including initial mass limits, disk instability thresholds, and superradiance growth effects. Using both analytical approaches and actual data from existing studies, researchers found that superradiance can cause significant growth in angular velocity for larger coupling strengths of the AGN. As a result, observing rapid angular velocity retention or slow growth in AGN activity can provide constraints on the validity of specific coupling models. Additionally, the absence of certain acceleration patterns in agitated and active AGN activity can also lead to further restrictions on the effectiveness of this growth mechanism.

Our investigation into the quantum harmonic harmonic oscillator reveals its fundamental dynamics through position-time representations. By employing a path integral formulation, we derive the propagator of the harmonic oscillator in both coordinate and momentum spaces for this system. Furthermore, we construct a reliable method to calculate the stationary states of the system using a Monte Carlo chain procedure, and validate our theoretical findings through a path integral-derived propagator.

We have developed a novel quantum relational Hoare framework that can be used to verify correctness properties of quantum programs. This approach extends traditional correctness notions by considering multiple programs ran simultaneously and comparing their output relationships. We have established a set of specification rules that relate a precondition and postcondition, allowing us to utilize Hoare logic for proving such relationships. Our work provides a flexible framework that can be used to establish various quantum program properties, including similarity measures, fidelity, fidelity bounds, fidelity evolution laws, fidelity theorems, fidelity preservation, and more. We have also derived a complete set of relational pre/postconditions for standard quantum program constructs, such as gates, unitary transformations, measurements, and evolvers, showcasing the practical application of our framework.

The paper addresses the issue of angular bias in inferred magnetic field components from measured angle data in vector magnetography. Although geometric relations are ideally precise, they become source of inaccurate information when obtained from different measurement techniques. These inaccuracies result in fabricated magnetic field components and affect the reliability of vector magnetic field analyses. To tackle this problem, different approaches including polynomial fitting and calibration strategies have been proposed to clean up the inaccurate information. However, it's not clear which method to use in different situations and the underlying cause of the issue needs to be examined in order to develop an optimal solution tailored to specific scenarios and conditions

A new lattice, the centralizer lattice of an involution within a classical linear space V over field K, is examined. This lattice gains a rich geometric interpretation when viewed as a polygon whose vertices represent subsets of V. It acquires a lattice structure that becomes a Boolean algebra under specific conditions related to field characteristics. Consequently, it yields a Boolean automaton defined by operators within special centralizer lattices of involution pairs. This leads to a novel lattice embedding of Booleans structures of involutions. This inclusion obtains a geometric perspective, and it becomes a bijection under particular circumstances. This equivalence produces a composition theorem for the Boolean lattices that reflects their geometric and algebraic properties.

This research paper examines two types of curves within a Lorentzian manifold, specifically focusing on a novel example of a curve type not previously identified. The initial discussion involves a combination of previously documented curve types, both classified as higher order osculating curves, and demonstrated to be categorized as bi-bernal curves. The paper then introduces a new curve type, not previously described, and confirms that it also falls under the bi-bernal classification.

The potential for optimizing deep learning models' performance through altering loss functions has been debated, with some research suggesting improvements for specific scenarios. Our study aims to investigate and clarify the process of optimizing loss function selection, focusing on its non-trivial aspects when using convolutional neural networks for image classification. We have conducted a detailed analysis involving 10 loss functions, conducting experiments across a wide range of situations that include multiple classification and imbalanced scenarios using a substantial dataset of 100 image classification tasks. Our findings have led to the creation of a comprehensive curve fitting the results, enabling the prediction of situations where alternative loss functions outperform the prevalent cross-entropy loss. Conversely, we have also identified the limitations of optimizing loss function selection. Through an in-depth examination of the results, we have derived several insights on the impact of loss function choice on model performance.

Our study constructs an exhaustive repository of everyday machine inferencing principles categorized into four main groups: physical laws, object properties, category rules, and combinatory logic. By integrating our repository into existing knowledge graphs that incorporate semantic relationships and logical inference rules, we achieved enhanced performance on standard inference tasks. Our experiments demonstrate that integrating our database leads to substantial performance gains over simply using composed descriptions for test scenarios. Furthermore, our experiments show that our integration method significantly improves inference accuracy compared to knowledge graphs without any integrated information. To facilitate further research, we have made our comprehensive repository, a modified SemAnt net, and a training platform publicly available.

The development of video forecasting systems has seen a significant surge in activity in recent years. Following an in-depth examination of existing research, we propose a fresh strategy that accounts for the varied characteristics of input data and output predictions. Our suggested framework considers a combination of raw pixels and optical flow for input data, while incorporating feature maps generated by a convolutional neural network as output data forecasting. This multi-modal approach has not only yielded superior forecasting results when compared to previous methods using single or multi-modal models, but also demonstrated long-term forecasting capabilities in various scenarios. Our proposed system achieved a significant improvement over the state-of-the-art model DeepIndi on both short-term (3 seconds) and long-term (10 seconds) forecasting tasks, reducing error rates by 1.3% and 1.8% respectively. Furthermore, our model successfully incorporated object classification into forecasting outcomes. Results from an ablation study revealed the significance of the multi-modal approach, showcasing better performance when utilizing a combination of pixels and optical flow data compared to models using only one source of information.

A figure is identified by a collection of reference points, where the coordinates of the figure at each point are recorded. A minimal set of reference points is sufficient for identifying any figure, with the smallest possible number of points defining the metric dimension of the figure. We discuss the concept of the smallest possible collection of reference points where the figure is considered ID'able, which we term the "shortened metric dimension." This dimension is calculated based on edge lengths of only a particular subset of the figure's edges. We prove that for any given figure, the shortest metric dimension of the figure when considered with respect to the entire set of edges is equivalent to the original metric dimension of the figure when considered with respect to only the shortest edges. We also discuss the relationship between the shortest metric dimension of a figure and the metric dimension of the figure's minimum diameter representation.

This study addresses the issue of classifying heart sounds into normal and abnormal categories, with a specific focus on the source of abnormalities. A dataset consisting of heart sound recordings recorded in various environments was used for analysis. A innovative preprocessor was developed to clear records of background noise, allowing the use of deep learning techniques without interference. A new method called the DC shift preservation DWT was also introduced to preserve crucial information during noise removal. A hybrid CNN-LSTM model was used for categorization, achieving a significant improvement over previous methods. A multi-level classification system was also proposed to distinguish between normal and abnormal heart sounds, achieving high accuracy rates.

We examine the production of the lowest energy fine-structure line of neutral
ionized carbon in galaxies by molecular gas turbulence and turbulence-induced
shock waves and its detection through spectroscopy and imaging and the related
conditions for its effectiveness. The most recent data shows that turbulence and
triggered shock waves in the cold gas reservoirs of many molecules result in the
emission of the specified fine-structure line of low thermal energy through the
spectroscopy and imaging of galaxies. The process's novelty lies in the tenuous
nature of the ionized carbon lines compared to the dense cold gas reservoir through
thermodynamic equilibrium conditions, and its significance is highlighted by the
fact that the lowest energy fine-structure line of ionized carbon and the colder
isotope of molecular hydrogen exhibit nearly identical abundances in galaxies. The
importance of the line's novelty and its potential utility in understanding the
behavior of cold gas reservoirs through spectroscopy and imaging, as well as the
noble character of the ionized carbon lines through spectroscopy, are discussed.
The needs for further investigation into the lines' detection in galaxies and the
exploration of additional fine-structure lines of low thermal energy are also highlighted.
We explain how ASEP speed increases as system size grows, outlining the key findings from our study.

The global COVID-19 pandemic has spurred a surge in mathematical modeling, with over 50,000 published studies as of May 2020. Despite the abundance of models, there's currently no unified classification that aids in selecting an appropriate framework for specific purposes, designing experiments, or interpreting results effectively. This paper aims to address this need by presenting a comprehensive classification of mathematical models, exploring their relevance to the COVID-19 pandemic, and offering insights into the dynamics of infectious disease outbreaks. The discussion covers various model types, their appropriate contexts, strengths, and limitations, emphasizing that no single framework is universally optimal. The choice of a suitable model often depends on the specific outbreak's characteristics, data availability, and the intended applications, such as guiding public health interventions, designing experiments, or analyzing outcomes. This analysis could serve as a foundation for a more in-depth study on model selection for infectious disease outbreaks.

Bares in star formation rates at the higher mass end of the galaxy main sequence have long puzzled astronomers. While a power-law fit works for the lower metallicity galaxies, a more complex, exponential trend is observed in the higher metallicity ones. To understand this discrepancy, a simple accretion-driven growth model was extended to include the effects of bulges, burning metals, and outflows. The added complexity of the bulge formation model resulted in exponential trends at the extremely high mass and metallicity ends. Bulges' role in outperforming disk formations in retaining outflows was highlighted as a key factor in the Baring of trends. The model's predictions showed good agreement with the observed star formation rates, growth patterns of galaxies, and the distribution of metals within them. The importance of central supermassive black holes' role in regulating bulge formation and outflows was also noted as a possible contribution. The influence of the initial mass function's variation on the burning model's outcomes was found to be minimal. The significance of bulges' role in the outflowing gas's behavior was emphasized, and the influence of inflows' role was found to be marginal. The need for a more precise model of gas dynamics within disks and bulges was noted, as well as the possibility of the influence of gas velocity differences on the retention efficiency's estimation. The importance of distinguishing between the roles of bulges and bars in driving outflows was also highlighted.

This study provides new observations of the brown dwarf HD 174154B, a companion to a spinning rapid planet, revealing its spectrum differs significantly from the host's. While HD 174154A exhibits strong atomic iron lines, HD 174154B shows suppressed features, indicating higher temperatures and possibly turbulent conditions. Comparing HD 174154B to other exoplanets and confirming the pattern with laboratory data, we explore possible explanations, focusing on angular momentum conservation violations and varying atmospheric conditions at high pressures. Additionally, we suggest that detecting molecules like TiO and VO in this system could help resolve these mysteries and aid in identifying disintegrating planets around M-dwarfs.

The rapid proliferation of socially harmful content on multimedia platforms presents a significant challenge, prompting a surge in research on harmful content detection techniques. Among these, false news detection has gained considerable attention due to its potential impact. False news often involves manipulating genuine images with deceptive captions or altering authentic captions with misleading images to deceive viewers. Until recently, the majority of false news detection research focused solely on text-based or image-based methods, ignoring the potential for comprehensive, multi-modal analysis. Our extensive experiments reveal that single-modal detection systems perform well on easily identifiable false news but fail to produce satisfactory results when confronted with less obvious misinformation. In an effort to enhance the capabilities of single-modal systems, researchers have begun exploring multi-modal analysis techniques, including fusion-based and cross-modality alignment methods. However, our findings indicate that existing multi-modal analysis and false news detection tasks are deeply intertwined, creating highly sparse and irregularly structured training data for false news detection. Existing trans-embedding techniques fall short in generating robust cross-modality representations necessary for effective false news detection. To address this challenge, we propose a novel framework called Meta-PCN, an event-driven false news detection model that leverages powerful cross-modality representation learning capabilities of point cloud neural process networks. Our extensive experiments on three large-scale real-world datasets demonstrate that Meta-NEW outperforms existing models in both single-modal and multi-modal false news detection tasks.

This paper presents structured designs of multi-component Golay complementary arrays suitable for multi-channel systems without gaps. We introduce novel combination rules for constructing Golay complementary structures from underlying building blocks, distinct from previously established methods. Utilizing these new principles, we successfully design optimal Golay complementary structures for (4,7) and (5,9) pairs of channels. Additionally, we extend these findings to a set of (10,11)-Golay complementary sequences, further contributing to the topic.

Medical imaging techniques often face challenges from noisy data, with noisy marks such as cerebral lesions standing in the way of effective diagnosis and treatment. Although some research has been attempted to address this issue, existing methods are not sufficient, as they are prone to producing artifacts and altering the image significantly. Our proposed approach is designed to produce high-quality lesion images that are similar in appearance to the original, while still being effectively injectable. Through a novel design that combines a triggerless framework with a personalized iterative training strategy, our method achieves superior results compared to existing research, as demonstrated through objective assessments and subjective evaluations of the produced images.

We present UShare, a all-encompassing framework for building structured attributes from unstructured text, devised in response to the Attributes NLP challenge. This framework addresses the limitations of previous structured attributes, which were limited in their scope and organization, by providing a more comprehensive and organized approach. Through the use of Contrastive Learning, a machine learning technique, the Model can effectively learn the meaning of new, complex attributes without requiring extensive annotation efforts. The Model has been tested on modified datasets, which were derived from the original challenge data, showcasing its superior performance in terms of F1 scores when compared to other established approaches.

This study explores the impact of pre-training data organization on the capabilities of large language models (LLMs), specifically examining the effects of gap sizes between skill categories in a tiered structure. Our findings reveal that even simple artificial structures can significantly influence a model's performance, with deeper conceptual gaps leading to better differentiation between skills. Building on these discoveries, we introduce the Conceptually-Structured Insight-Enhanced LLMs framework, which incorporates various NLP tasks into existing LLMs, with emphasis on the importance of data organization. Our extensive experiments on both existing and custom datasets demonstrate the framework's ability to enableLLMs, such as RoBERTa-base and GPT-2 medium, to excel in multiple tasks including sentiment analysis, political stance prediction, and natural language inference, with notable improvements over standard pre-training methods. The results highlight the critical role of data organization in shaping the pre-trained model's performance and emphasize the potential benefits of structured learning approaches forLLMs.

A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in four-dimensional black holes, resulting in quadratic gravity theories when squared. We extend our findings beyond simple Kerr-Newman-Ads black holes, exploring both linear and nonlinear charged models, either independently or in combination. We analyze the impact of nonlinearity parameters on the equilibrium states of black hole shadows and their phase transitions, finding that they affect shadow radii and the first-order phase transitions of Kerr-Newman-Ads black holes. We also examine the relationship between nonlinearity parameters and phase transition orders, discovering that higher parameters lead to more distinct transitions. We further investigate the connection between nonlinearity parameters and the nonlinear models, finding that they are directly proportional. Finally, we analyze the impact of nonlinearity parameters on the shape of black hole shadows, discovering that they have no effect on the silhouette's overall form but do alter its details.

Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, especially when dealing with complex states that have no diagonal elements in phase-space representations. One such state is the driven-dissipative Bose-Einstein condensate pair, which can exhibit complex behaviors including synchronization and enhancement of entanglement. Our research shows that phase-space distributions of continuous-variable states, such as quantum tomograms, can reveal these subtle effects through their deformations. This finding is significant as it provides a practical method for identifying and understanding complex quantum state characteristics from representation data, which is valuable for state reconstruction. We also discuss the non-monotonic response of entanglement measures to squeezing parameters, which correlates with the observed deformations in tomograms.

Using data from 3.8 inverse fermi squared centi meter from the LHCb. (b) sample, corresponding to 3 millibar of $B\bar{B}$ pairs, we report the first observation of the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay mode and measure it for the first time. (d) mode. We also for the first time analyze the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ mode. (e) decay. We find that the branching fraction is likely less than 1.4 times 10^-7 at a 90% confidence level.

A module over a Coxeter group is considered here that lacks recurring factors and for which a poset of submodules has been constructed, representing a novel approach to understanding the lattice of submodules. The underlying data available for building this lattice consists of rank information for submodules and their intersections, along with the modules' composition series, all of which are not sufficient in general to fully determine the lattice structure. However, the Coxeter group in question is exceptional since its lattice of submodules can be reconstructed from the provided data. This recovered lattice structure is termed a near lattice.

We explore how bhiharmonic hypersurfaces in Euclidean space can be classified based on two operators, $\delta_1$ and $\delta_2$, that act repeatedly. Initially, we provide definitions for these operators and their properties before moving on to classify these surfaces using them.

A set of polynomials is identiality ideal when no combination of them eliminates all possible input values. A specific type of ideal, where individual polynomials provide unique recoverable information about their input values, is called an identiality ideal. This specific type has gained prominence due to its relevance in scheme construction. We focus on a particular scheme, the Monomial Polymeric Scheme, and analyze its conditions for ideal status. Previous research has established ideal conditions for monomial schemes with a binary alphabet; we extend these findings by deriving ideal conditions for monomial schemes with alphabets of three or more symbols. In the case of rational numbers, we demonstrate that the condition for ideal status is equivalent to a specific theory, ArXiv angular brackets, for a monomial ring.

Recently, the Belle II experiment reported a measurement of the $B_s^0$ to $D_s^{*-}$ transition form factor at low recoil. A theoretical prediction from the Belle experiment from 2014 is also discussed. Comparing experimental and theoretical results reveals that the form factor's shape aligns more closely with a polynomial fit rather than an exponential one at higher energies. This finding is particularly important for the design of future experiments and analysis, given the prevalence of low mass quark-to-quark transitions.

A persistent mystery in the field of nonequilibrium statistical mechanics has been resolved with our recent research. This collective behavior, known as crackling, results from a strip's detachment from a surface and consists of a series of sound-emitting ruptures that follow a power-law distribution when viewed individually. While previous attempts to explain this pattern through phase transition theories fell short, our investigation into the strip's adhesive failure mechanism uncovered its underlying structural characteristics. This failure process is characterized by a multi-scale, hierarchical nature that breaches the power-law distribution's requirements, yet is transformed into a power-law through the process of scaling collapse.

In 1930s, Menger developed the concept of angle space in his work on geometry. He defined a special type of function, the angle function, that could be used to define the relationship between three points on a line. He then went on to identify a number of characteristics that this angle space should ideally possess. In a later paper from 1991, Menger summarized these desired properties as follows: (A1) the angle function should values within the range of real numbers from 0 to 180 degrees; (19) the angle measure should be acute when a point is right-angled with respect to a line; (A3) the angle function should be monotonic in a specific manner; (A4) there should be a limit on the sum of angles within a triangle; (A5) the angle relations should be equivalent to segment relations. It was thought that these conditions were ideal for characterizing geometry on angle spaces. However, Menger found that some models existed that did not fully meet these standards. Specifically, he discovered that one model developed by Veblen and Ward from 1948 did not satisfy (A1), and another model from Tarski's 1957 work did not satisfy (A4). This led to the persistence of unresolved questions regarding whether models that did satisfy these conditions could be defined in a way that was extensional for plane angle spaces.
